\begin{abstract}
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs) distribute adversarial intent across seemingly benign conversational turns and evade per-turn safety filters.
Standard temporal classifiers fail to generalize: a vanilla DeBERTa encoder achieves only F1\,=\,0.28 on out-of-distribution (OOD) attack types unseen during training.
We design six controlled variants of a DeBERTa-based detection framework to systematically decompose what enables cross-attack generalization.

Domain-adaptive pretraining bridges the entire +72 percentage point OOD gap; classification supervision is non-essential for detection, while misaligned supervision actively impedes generalization.
Persuasion-aware classification contributes beyond detection in two ways: it provides zero degradation under adversarial perturbation (vs. 2.6 percentage points for MLM), and its 9-class taxonomy yields distinct strategy trajectories per attack type for human-interpretable analysis.
These results reframe multi-turn jailbreak detection as a domain adaptation problem rather than a classification design problem.
\end{abstract}

% conclusion.tex — D019+D020+D021+D022 Reframe

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented DisPeD, a two-stage DeBERTa-based framework with six controlled Stage~1 variants that systematically decompose what enables cross-attack generalization in multi-turn jailbreak detection.
The central finding is that jailbreak-domain continued pretraining bridges the entire +72 percentage point OOD gap (vanilla F1\,=\,0.28 $\to$ adapted F1\,$\geq$\,0.99), and classification supervision is non-essential for detection: the MLM-only variant achieves F1\,=\,1.00 on unseen Deceptive Delight without any labels.
Domain specificity is confirmed: Wikipedia MLM with matched token count reaches only F1\,=\,0.74, comparable to misaligned topic classification (F1\,=\,0.73), and far below jailbreak-domain MLM (F1\,=\,1.00).
Generic continued pretraining provides partial improvement (+46 percentage points over vanilla) but fails to bridge the full gap.
These results reframe multi-turn jailbreak detection as a jailbreak-domain adaptation problem rather than a classification design problem.

Persuasion-aware classification contributes beyond detection in two independent dimensions.
The 9-class model achieves zero degradation under adversarial perturbation (vs.\ 2.6 percentage points for MLM-only and 11.8 for vanilla), providing robustness that unsupervised domain exposure alone does not guarantee.
Its persuasion taxonomy also yields distinct strategy trajectory signatures per attack type (e.g., Crescendo's broad transition coverage vs.\ FITD's concentrated role-assignment pattern), enabling security analysts to inspect \emph{why} conversations are flagged without post-hoc explanation methods.
Domain exposure drives detection; classification supervision adds robustness and interpretability.

Several limitations constrain the conclusions.
First, the dataset is small (500 training and 160 OOD test conversations), and these results require validation at larger scale.
Second, all conversations were generated by Qwen3-8B; human adversaries may exhibit different attack characteristics that synthetic data does not capture.
Third, DisPeD detects persuasion presence per turn, so attacks that distribute persuasion sparsely across many turns might evade the detector.
Fourth, TF-IDF achieves F1\,=\,0.944 on Deceptive Delight; DisPeD's advantage over bag-of-words is strongest under adversarial perturbation and for interpretability.
Fifth, only persuasion-mediated attacks fall within scope; token smuggling, pure information accumulation, and single-frame roleplay operate through orthogonal mechanisms.

Future work should evaluate on human-generated attacks, scale to larger multi-source datasets spanning more attack families, and test robustness against adaptive attacks that target the domain-specific features directly.
Integration with production safety systems as a complementary multi-turn detection layer is a natural deployment path.
